source.title: Deep sparse autoencoders yield interpretable features too

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE features in an LLM are interpretable using automated explanation and activation-prediction scores, rather than directly measuring feature geometry.
record.gate_note: The post also reports a reconstruction-sparsity comparison and dead-neuron rates, but those measures do not test the listed claim versions. Figure 3 gives the interpretability results without numeric values in the supplied text; the author describes the scores comparatively.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on GPT2-small and compares deep and shallow SAE architectures by automated interpretability. That is a comparison of its own method against the standard one. No score is reported numerically, and there is no non-SAE baseline such as neurons or random directions. No rate or strength of superposition or feature recovery is measured. The link to superposition is only the author's argument, which the author hedges with an alternative linear-superposition explanation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes deep SAEs yield features on par with shallow SAEs in automated interpretability. He explicitly declines to claim either architecture is more interpretable, because of large dead-neuron differences. He argues superposition may not fully explain SAE success, while offering a linear-superposition explanation and saying results do not strongly confirm his intuition.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of the toy-model method: it trains deep and shallow SAEs on GPT2-small activations and evaluates feature interpretability.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE depth was associated with more dead features; the author identifies dead-neuron differences as a confound for comparing interpretability scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Deep SAEs, with nonlinear non-sparse layers around the sparse layer, yield features scored at least as interpretable as shallow SAE features (Fig. 3). The author argues this is unlikely if superposition alone explains SAE success. The author also concedes a linear-superposition account: grouping and ungrouping of co-occurring features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The interpretability of SAE features is not by itself evidence for linear superposition, since nonlinear deep SAEs also yield interpretable features.

record.problems: The reported interpretability scores are presented in a figure without numeric values in the supplied text. The author notes that dead-neuron differences are a confound and that dead-neuron frequency almost certainly affects automated interpretability scores. The author also notes that parameter count was not controlled across architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Reconstruction-sparsity results and dead-neuron percentages are not rows because they do not directly measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Whether GPT2-small's features are spread across neurons, and whether SAE features are more interpretable than neurons or random baselines (no non-SAE baseline; scores figure-only).
Completeness, stability and canonical status of SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: Blog post (LessWrong/Alignment Forum), not peer-reviewed. The reader's V4 'supports' label was removed: the rows compare SAE architectures and give no figure-readable values or non-SAE baseline. The reconstruction-sparsity and dead-neuron results are also method-performance measures. Commenters note that dead features are excluded from the autointerp pipeline.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes neuron polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Does not directly establish that SAE features are the model's underlying features or measure how features are distributed across the target model's neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonical status of SAE features.
Whether the model's represented features are one-dimensional directions.
